q: The 32-bit value 0x0A0B0C0D is written to memory on a little-endian machine. What is the byte sequence, lowest address first?
exp: Little-endian stores the least significant byte at the lowest address. The least significant byte of 0x0A0B0C0D is 0x0D, so the order is 0D 0C 0B 0A — a straight reversal of the bytes. Option (a) is the big-endian layout. Option (c) swaps within pairs only, a common distractor.

q: Which scheduling algorithm gives provably minimum average waiting time?
exp: SJF is optimal for average waiting time — this can be proved by an exchange argument: swapping any adjacent pair so the shorter job runs first never increases total waiting time. q: Thrashing in a virtual memory system refers to

opts.A: Physical damage to disk platters from repeated seeking
opts.B: A process spending more time servicing page faults than executing

q: The Banker's algorithm is used for deadlock

q: Which cache write policy updates main memory only when the modified cache block is evicted, reducing memory traffic but risking data loss on power failure?

q: The Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) improves virtual memory performance by:

opts.A: Storing recently used page-table entries so most address translations skip the extra memory access to the page table
opts.B: Reserving a dedicated physical frame for every process
opts.D: Compressing page-table entries so the whole table fits in cache

exp: The TLB is a small, fast associative cache of recent virtual-to-physical page mappings. A hit avoids the extra memory access needed to walk the page table; a miss forces a page-table walk (potentially multiple memory accesses for a multi-level table), after which the result is cached in the TLB. Do not confuse a TLB miss (translation not cached, but the page may well be resident in memory) with a page fault (the page is not in memory at all) — they trigger very different handling.

q: Compared with SRAM, DRAM is:

opts.A: Faster and needs no periodic refresh, which is why it is used for cache
opts.B: Slower and requires periodic refreshing, but denser and cheaper, which is why it is used for main memory
opts.C: Non-volatile, which is why it is used for BIOS firmware

q: The key distinction between a mutex lock and a binary semaphore is that:

opts.A: A mutex can take more than two values, a binary semaphore cannot
opts.B: A mutex has ownership — only the thread that locked it may unlock it — while a binary semaphore has no such restriction
opts.C: Semaphores are used only for mutual exclusion, mutexes only for signalling between threads
opts.D: Mutexes always require busy-waiting, semaphores never do

exp: A mutex is owned by whichever thread acquired it; only that thread may release it. A binary semaphore is just a 0/1 counter with no ownership — any thread can signal it, even one that never waited on it, which is exactly what makes semaphores useful for signalling between threads (e.g. producer–consumer), not just exclusion. Busy-waiting vs blocking is an implementation choice available to either construct, so option (d) is not a valid general distinction.

q: Memory-mapped file I/O (e.g. via mmap() on Unix) allows a process to:

opts.A: Access a file's contents directly through ordinary memory load/store instructions, with the OS transparently paging data in and out
opts.B: Bypass the file system entirely and write straight to raw disk sectors
opts.C: Guarantee a file stays fully resident in RAM until the process exits

exp: mmap() maps a file's contents into the calling process's virtual address space; ordinary memory reads/writes then transparently trigger the OS's paging mechanism to fetch or flush data, avoiding explicit read()/write() calls and letting multiple processes share the mapping as a form of IPC. It does not guarantee full residency — mapped pages are evicted and reloaded on demand just like any other page, which is why remnants of a memory-mapped document can end up in the pagefile/swap even though the user never explicitly saved it.
